User Stories and Epics: Why the Slice Matters and the Sentence Mostly Does Not

Two product leaders, one selling regulated enterprise software into hospitals and one selling a metal box with firmware inside it to forty-one thousand shopkeepers, arrive at the same January planning meeting with the same textbook and reach opposite conclusions about how to cut their work apart. Both are right. Understanding why is the difference between a practitioner who can recite INVEST and one who can referee an argument about it.

1. Two planning rooms, one week apart

On Monday 12 January 2026, Arvind Bhatnagar, VP of Product at Granthik Health Systems in Hyderabad, took a whiteboard marker to a problem that his four squads had already failed to size twice. Granthik sells a hospital information system and revenue-cycle suite to sixty-one hospitals across eleven chains, most of them running the software on servers inside their own basements. Annual recurring revenue was a little over ₹96 crore, and roughly a third of it sat with four chains that had, in the previous eighteen months, all begun asking the same question: when would Granthik connect their cashless insurance pre-authorisation flow to the National Health Claims Exchange, the interoperability layer the National Health Authority had been pushing through the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission, so that a hospital's admissions desk could file one pre-auth in one format rather than eleven insurer portals with eleven quirks each? One chain, nine hospitals across Telangana and Andhra, had put a date in a renewal contract: live by 1 April 2026.

Arvind's constraint was not capacity. His four squads, twenty-seven engineers, had a combined sustained throughput of about ninety-two story points per two-week sprint, and the coarse estimate for the pre-authorisation work was around 140 points. Five sprints to a code freeze on 6 March left him, arithmetically, with slack. His constraint was that Granthik shipped on-premises, on a quarterly release train, to hospitals whose IT staff scheduled upgrades around surgery calendars. The gap between an engineer merging a change and any real hospital clerk touching it averaged ninety-four days. Whatever Arvind cut his epic into, he would not learn whether the cut was right until long after the cutting was done. The textbook told him to slice thin and learn fast. He had done the second half of that sentence exactly zero times in six years at Granthik.

Seven days later, on Monday 19 January, Sneha Kulkarni sat in a different kind of room in Bengaluru, with a different kind of problem and the same textbook. Sneha was Director of Product at Gadya Retail Devices, a company that manufactured in Coimbatore and wrote software in Bengaluru: its product was the Gadya Tol, a counter terminal combining a weighing platform, a thermal printer and an Android billing head, sold to kirana stores and produce retailers, backed by a cloud dashboard and a companion app that helped shopkeepers with GST filings. Forty-one thousand terminals were in the field. The feature on Sneha's desk was deceptively small: let the shopkeeper accept a UPI payment on the terminal itself and reconcile it automatically against the bill just printed, instead of the current ritual of a static QR sticker on the wall, a phone held up to confirm, and a manual tick in the ledger.

The feature touched three systems on three different clocks. The cloud reconciliation service shipped weekly. The companion app shipped fortnightly through the app stores. The terminal firmware shipped three times a year — February, June and October — because pushing an over-the-air update to forty-one thousand devices sitting on patchy connectivity in Salem, Bhatinda and Barasat was a genuinely dangerous operation, and because anything that touched the weighing path dragged in Legal Metrology re-verification and a BIS conformance question that had once cost Gadya seven weeks. Sneha's slicing problem was not "how small can I make this." It was "which of these three clocks does each slice have to catch, and what happens to the slices that miss."

Both leaders had read Mike Cohn. Both could recite INVEST. By Friday of that week Arvind had split his epic twenty-two ways and Sneha had refused to split hers at all below the firmware boundary, and both decisions were defensible. The rest of this page is an argument about why.

2. The idea, stated precisely — and the four schools that disagree about it

A user story is a unit of work defined by a change in what some identified user can do, sized so that a team can design, build, verify and demonstrate it inside one iteration, and specified deliberately incompletely so that the detail is settled by conversation at the moment of building rather than by document at the moment of planning. An epic is a story that has not yet been cut down to that size: a holding container for an outcome the organisation has agreed matters, carrying no separate budget, schedule or owner of its own.

That is the definition. The argument this page makes about it is narrower and more contestable, and it is worth putting on the table before the history rather than after:

The central claim. Everything durable in the practice of user stories comes from the properties of the slice — its size, its independence, its demonstrability, its falsifiability. Everything contested comes from the apparatus — the sentence template, story points, the epic hierarchy, who holds the pen. Experts abandon the apparatus freely and the slice properties almost never. The reason is that the slice does two distinct jobs — it shortens the interval between a decision and its refutation, and it reduces the variance of any forecast built on it — and only the first of those two jobs depends on being able to ship to real users quickly. Where feedback is structurally slow, as at Granthik and inside Gadya's firmware, the first job disappears and the second remains. Practitioners who cannot tell those two jobs apart argue past each other permanently.

Where the practice came from

The story format emerged from the Extreme Programming work Kent Beck and Ward Cunningham did at Chrysler in the late 1990s, and its original enemy was specific: the requirements document that was exhaustive, expensive to maintain, contractual in tone, and stale by the time an engineer opened it. Beck's move was to shrink the written artefact until it could no longer pretend to be complete, thereby forcing the conversation it had been substituting for. Ron Jeffries gave the practice its most quoted formulation — card, conversation, confirmation, the three C's — in which the card is only a token, the conversation is the real specification, and the confirmation is the agreed test. Mike Cohn's User Stories Applied (2004) then did the systematising work that made the practice teachable: the role–goal–benefit template, relative estimation in story points, planning poker, and the INVEST heuristic — Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable — which is still the single most useful diagnostic in the field and also the most widely misapplied.

What is usually left out of this potted history is that the practice was designed for a particular delivery physics: a small co-located team, a single deployable codebase, a customer in the room, and a release cycle measured in weeks. Every serious disagreement in the field since 2004 is a disagreement about what survives when one of those four conditions is removed.

The four schools, and the proposition each will and will not sign

The conversation school descends directly from Jeffries and Beck. It holds that written detail beyond a reminder is waste, that the story is a promise of a conversation, and that a team which writes elaborate stories has reinvented the requirements document with worse typography. It will sign: "the written story should be the smallest artefact that reliably triggers the right conversation." It will not sign: "the story text is the specification," nor "a story can be handed to an offshore team and built without the author present." Its evidence is the repeated observation that heavyweight written requirements do not prevent misunderstanding, they only relocate the blame for it.

The specification-by-example school, associated with Dan North's behaviour-driven development and Gojko Adzic's later work, holds almost the opposite on the question that matters: that the acceptance examples are the requirement, that Given/When/Then is not decoration but the executable heart of the story, and that a conversation whose output is not written down as concrete examples has not happened in any recoverable sense. It will sign: "a story is not ready until three or four concrete examples with real values exist." It will not sign: "detail is waste." Its evidence is the class of defect that arises not from misunderstanding the goal but from never having agreed a boundary value — and the observation that in regulated and enterprise contexts, the examples are the only thing an auditor, a QA lead or a customer's technical contact can actually read.

The flow school — Kanban lineage, David Anderson and Daniel Vacanti on one side, the #NoEstimates argument of Woody Zuill and Vasco Duarte on the other — attacks the estimation apparatus rather than the writing. It holds that story points are a costly proxy for something you can simply measure: if you right-size every item so that it finishes within some percentile of your historical cycle-time distribution, then counting items forecasts as well as summing points, and Little's Law gives you more planning leverage than velocity ever will. It will sign: "right-size, then count throughput." It will not sign: "velocity is a planning instrument," and it is openly hostile to "velocity is a performance measure." Its evidence is empirical: across many teams, the correlation between point totals and elapsed time is not meaningfully better than the correlation between item counts and elapsed time.

The structure school covers two otherwise antagonistic camps that share one belief: that the flat backlog of stories loses something essential. Jeff Patton's story mapping argues the lost thing is narrative — the left-to-right sequence of what a user actually does, against which a release is a horizontal slice rather than a prefix of a sorted list. The scaled-framework camp, of which SAFe is the most deployed example, argues the lost thing is economic hierarchy: above a certain organisational size you need explicit levels — portfolio epic, capability, feature, story — with funding decisions at the top and sequencing arithmetic such as weighted shortest job first to connect them. Patton will not sign "epics are a useful container"; he regards the epic/story hierarchy as an accounting artefact that destroys the map. SAFe will not sign "each team invents its own splitting patterns"; it regards local variation above a certain scale as an integration hazard. Both will sign: "a sorted list of stories is not a plan."

There is also a persistent minority dissent worth naming because experienced practitioners quietly hold it: the job story variant popularised at Intercom, which discards the persona clause entirely in favour of when [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [outcome], on the grounds that "as a Class 12 aspirant" or "as a fleet dispatcher" smuggles in a confidence about who the user is that the team has not earned, whereas the situation is observable. Arvind, as it happens, had adopted this form for Granthik's stories two years earlier without telling anyone it had a name.

3. Mechanics in depth: what expert practitioners actually do

The textbook sequence — name the epics, write the stories, attach acceptance criteria, apply INVEST, split, estimate, order — is accurate as far as it goes, and a competent practitioner executes it. What separates the expert is a set of steps that sit between those steps and are almost never written down. There are four, and each has a second-order effect that the naive version does not anticipate.

Step zero: establish the slice's clock before choosing its size

Before Arvind cut anything, he did an exercise that took him forty minutes and that most teams skip entirely: for each layer of the system, he wrote down the elapsed time between an engineer merging a change and any real user's behaviour producing a signal about it. For Granthik's web tier behind a feature flag at a pilot hospital, four days. For the same tier at a non-pilot hospital on the quarterly train, ninety-four days. For a database migration touching historical claims, one hundred and eighty days, because the affected records only surfaced at quarter-end reconciliation. Sneha did the same for Gadya: two days for the cloud reconciliation service, sixteen days for the companion app, one hundred and twenty-one days for firmware, and for anything crossing the Legal Metrology boundary, effectively a full season.

This matters because the argument for thin slices has two independent legs and they pay out on different clocks. The learning leg — ship small, find out you were wrong, change course — is worth almost nothing when the feedback interval is one hundred and twenty-one days, because you will have finished the whole epic before the first signal arrives. The variance leg — small items make forecasts tighter and integration failures cheaper — pays out regardless of feedback latency. An expert who has done step zero will slice a firmware epic thinly for the second reason while being honest that the first reason does not apply, and will therefore not waste political capital promising leadership that thin slicing will "let us learn fast." That promise, made in a context where it cannot be kept, is one of the most reliable ways a product manager destroys their own credibility.

Step one and a half: split along a seam, then check the seam against ownership

The splitting patterns practitioners reach for are well catalogued — workflow steps, business-rule variants, data boundaries, interface variations, CRUD operations, happy path before error cases, and the quality-attribute split that separates "works for ten concurrent users" from "works for four thousand." The implicit step is checking the resulting seam against the org chart. A split that produces two beautifully independent stories owned by two different squads has not reduced coordination cost; it has converted an intra-team problem into an inter-team one, which is usually more expensive. Arvind's pre-authorisation epic had exactly this shape: the NHCX payload construction sat with the Integrations squad, the admissions-desk interface with Clinical Workflows, and the audit trail with Platform. His first split produced eleven stories spread across three squads with a dependency graph that his delivery manager described, accurately, as a plate of noodles.

What Arvind did next is the expert move. Rather than splitting further, he re-cut the epic along a different axis: instead of splitting by system layer, he split by insurer. The first three stories delivered the full end-to-end pre-auth flow — payload, interface, audit — for a single insurer with a single procedure category. Each story now sat mostly inside one squad, because one squad could be temporarily loaned the two engineers it needed, and each was demonstrable to a hospital clerk. Total points went up. Coordination went down. This is the trade the textbook does not make explicit: splitting trades total effort for reduced variance and reduced coordination, and the exchange rate is worth measuring for your own team.

Forty-one percent is a large number and it demands an explanation rather than an apology. Part of it is real: each slice carries its own test harness, its own feature flag, its own deployment verification, and in Granthik's case its own audit-log entry format. Part of it is measurement artefact: engineers estimate a vague thing optimistically and a specific thing realistically, so a chunk of the "inflation" is the coarse estimate having been wrong. Both parts have a second-order consequence that trips up leaders reading a velocity chart. Because the points inflate but the underlying work does not inflate by the same amount, velocity rises after a team adopts disciplined splitting — Granthik's rose about eighteen percent over two quarters — and any executive who reads that as a productivity gain has been misled by an accounting change. Arvind pre-empted this by writing the inflation number into the plan document before anyone could discover it later.

The variance argument, worked

The formal case for "Small" in INVEST is not an aesthetic preference; it is a statement about the standard deviation of a sum. Suppose a sprint's committed work is composed of n items of roughly equal size whose individual actual efforts are independent with coefficient of variation c — that is, each item's standard deviation is c times its mean. Then the standard deviation of the total, expressed as a fraction of the committed total, is simply c divided by the square root of n. The size of the items cancels out. Only the count matters.

The step most teams skip entirely: right-sizing from your own cycle-time distribution

The flow school's contribution here is practical and underused. Gadya's cloud squad pulled six months of history — one hundred and eighteen completed stories — and looked not at points but at elapsed cycle time: median three days, eighty-fifth percentile eleven days, ninety-fifth percentile twenty-six days. Sneha's team then adopted a rule that replaced most of their estimation ceremony: any story that the team believed would take longer than eleven days either got split or got a time-boxed spike attached to reduce its uncertainty first. Little's Law supplied the other half of the discipline. With nine items in progress and a throughput of four and a half items per week, average cycle time was two weeks; cutting work in progress to four items dropped it under a week without any change to how fast anyone worked. Expert practitioners reach for that lever before they reach for a better estimate, because it is the only one that reliably moves.

4. When the practice applies, and when it is actively misleading

The conditions under which story slicing pays can be stated as testable claims rather than as advice. Four of them matter, and it is instructive to apply each to both protagonists.

Claim one: the work can be cut so that each piece changes observable behaviour for an identifiable user. True for Granthik's pre-auth epic — each insurer-by-procedure slice changes what a specific admissions clerk sees and does. Largely false for a class of Gadya's work: a firmware change that reduces the terminal's cold-boot time from nineteen seconds to eleven is genuinely valuable to forty-one thousand shopkeepers and cannot be sliced into behaviour-changing pieces at all, because nine-tenths of the improvement lives in a single boot-sequence rewrite. Where claim one fails, insisting on user stories produces fiction: teams invent "as a shopkeeper I want the boot loader refactored" and everyone involved knows it is theatre.

Claim two: the cost of integrating n slices is materially less than n times the cost of integrating one. True in a continuously deployed web service with good test automation. Sharply false across Gadya's firmware boundary, where each additional firmware candidate requires a regression pass on eleven hardware revisions, a staged OTA rollout, and, if the weighing path is touched, external verification. For Sneha, the integration cost per slice is close to constant and large, which is precisely why she refused to split below the firmware boundary: five firmware slices would have cost five verification cycles to deliver one feature.

Claim three: feedback from a shipped slice arrives soon enough to change the next slice. True for Gadya's cloud tier, false for Granthik's on-prem train unless a pilot exists. Arvind's response was to manufacture the condition rather than abandon the practice: he negotiated a two-hospital pilot inside the nine-hospital chain with a fortnightly update cadence, which pulled his feedback latency from ninety-four days to nineteen for the slices that mattered most. This is what expert judgement looks like — not choosing between the practice and the constraint, but spending political capital to relax the constraint where the practice is worth the most.

Claim four: the value of a slice is roughly independent of the slices not yet built. This is INVEST's "Valuable" and it is the claim that fails most often and most invisibly. A two-sided flow, a compliance obligation and a hardware-plus-software feature all share the property that partial delivery is worth zero or less than zero. Granthik's audit-trail stories were a clean example: half an audit trail is not half as useful as a whole one, it is a liability, because a hospital's compliance officer reviewing a partial trail may reasonably conclude the system is unreliable. Arvind therefore kept four audit stories in one sprint and one release, sliced for variance but released as a set — a distinction the textbook blurs and experts hold firmly.

Where the practice becomes actively misleading is worth stating plainly. It misleads when the real question is whether to build something rather than in what order, because the story format has nothing to say about that and its comforting concreteness can make a badly chosen feature feel rigorously planned. It misleads when the product's quality is a distributional property rather than a behavioural one, which is the AI-native case taken up below. And it misleads whenever "the backlog is groomed" is offered as evidence that a strategy exists.

5. Hard edge cases and what mature companies actually do

Two-sided and marketplace products

On a marketplace, a supply-side story that ships without its matching demand-side story changes nothing anyone experiences, which means INVEST's "Independent" and "Valuable" are in direct tension. The honest resolution used by mature marketplace teams is a paired story with a single acceptance boundary and an explicit sequencing note: the supply story may merge first, but neither is "done" until the pair is demonstrable together. The dishonest resolution, common enough to be worth recognising, is to declare the supply story done, bank the points, and let the demand story slip into the next sprint — which makes velocity look healthy while user-visible progress is exactly zero. The tell is a burn-up chart that rises smoothly while the product metric it was supposed to move stays flat for two quarters.

Regulated products

Granthik's situation generalises. In regulated software, some acceptance criteria are not negotiable at all — they are restatements of an external obligation, and the "N" in INVEST simply does not apply to them. Mature teams in health, insurance and lending handle this by separating two kinds of criteria on the same story: the behavioural criteria, which the team may negotiate, and the conformance criteria, which are traced to a clause in a circular or a specification and which a regulator's auditor may later read. Granthik tagged the second kind with the source document reference directly in the story, a practice that looked like bureaucratic clutter until the chain's compliance team asked, in February, for evidence of consent-artefact handling and Arvind produced it from the backlog in under an hour. What mature companies say they do is "we write user stories like everyone else." What they actually do is maintain a parallel traceability spine and hang stories off it.

Hardware plus software

Sneha's two-clock problem is the general form. The move that works, and that Gadya adopted for the UPI-on-terminal feature, is to pull the variable behaviour off the slow clock. Rather than encoding the UPI flow in firmware, her team shipped a firmware change that was deliberately minimal and generic — expose a secure display surface and a payment-event callback that the Android billing head could drive — and put every piece of product judgement into the app and cloud layers, which ship weekly. The firmware slice was large, singular and conservative; the software slices above it were numerous, thin and revisable. This is the hardware analogue of a platform decision, and it cost about forty percent more engineering than encoding the flow directly in firmware would have. Sneha's argument for the premium was not elegance: it was that a wrong decision encoded in firmware would be uncorrectable until June at the earliest, and the expected cost of being wrong exceeded the premium.

AI-native products

Gaatha Voice, a Bengaluru company selling a voice agent that handles collections and servicing calls for non-banking finance companies, ran into the deepest version of the problem. Its head of product, Ritwik Mohanty, split an epic — "the agent handles a request to change a payment date, end to end" — into seven INVEST-compliant stories: recognise the intent, confirm the loan account, check eligibility against the lender's rules, propose a new date, capture consent, write to the servicing system, confirm in the caller's language. Every story shipped. Every story passed its acceptance criteria. Over four sprints, containment — the proportion of calls resolved without a human — fell from fifty-eight percent to forty-one.

The failure is instructive because nothing in the process was done badly. The stories were small, independent, testable and demonstrable. The problem is that the quality of a conversational agent is not a property of any individual behaviour; it is a property of the joint distribution of behaviours across the space of real calls. Each slice, tested in isolation against three or four crafted examples, passed; composed, they produced an agent that asked for confirmation four times in a two-minute call and that callers hung up on. Behavioural specification — the entire premise of the acceptance criterion — assumes the system is a function you can test pointwise. A model is not.

The organisational seam

All four edge cases share a structural feature, which Figure 3 makes concrete: the slice that is right for the user cuts across the boundary that is right for the organisation. Every serious company resolves this the same way in practice, whatever its framework says — by nominating one squad as the integrating owner of the epic, giving it the right to pull engineers temporarily from the others, and accepting that the resulting stories are independent only within that squad's horizon. Frameworks call this a feature team. Practitioners call it "whoever holds the pager for the demo."

6. Ten distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The template is the least important part of the practice. An expert will write a story titled "Insurer rejection reasons shown verbatim on the pre-auth card, not mapped to our own codes" and nobody in the room will object, because the title carries a decision and the decision is the point. The tell-tale sign is a backlog in which some items use the role–goal–benefit form and some do not, with the form appearing exactly where the user identity is genuinely in question. The obvious reading — that this is sloppiness — is wrong; the template's value is that it forces you to name a user and a benefit, and once those are settled and shared, repeating them in every title is ritual.

"Independent" almost never means independent. It means sequenceable without rework. The expert's question is never "can these be built in any order" but "if we ship only this one and stop, what do we have to undo?" The tell-tale sign is a practitioner who accepts a hard dependency without discomfort but reacts sharply to a story that would require rewriting a data model if the next story never arrives. The obvious reading of INVEST produces artificial splits whose only virtue is that they can be listed separately.

Splitting costs effort, and the exchange rate is a measurable local constant. An expert can quote their own team's inflation figure — Arvind's was forty-one percent, Sneha's cloud squad ran nearer twenty-two — and uses it to decide when to stop. The tell is someone declining a further split on explicitly quantitative grounds rather than on feel. The obvious reading, that smaller is always better, ignores Figure 2's flattening tail.

Acceptance criteria are a falsifiability contract, not a completeness exercise. Their purpose is to give a tester something that can fail. The tell is an expert deleting criteria from a story — removing three that merely restated the definition of done, keeping two that name boundary values. The obvious reading, that more criteria are safer, produces lists so long that nobody reads them, at which point they protect nothing.

Story points are a conversation protocol whose numeric output is the least valuable thing it produces. The value is in the moment two engineers show a 3 and a 13 and have to explain themselves, because the spread localises a hidden assumption. The tell is a facilitator who, on seeing a wide spread, stops the round to extract the disagreement and then accepts almost any number afterwards. The obvious reading treats the number as the deliverable, which is how planning poker degenerates into fifteen minutes of arithmetic theatre.

Velocity is a capacity measurement and stops being one the moment it becomes a performance measurement. Goodhart's law operates here with unusual speed: point inflation is undetectable from outside and requires no dishonesty, only optimism. The tell is an expert who refuses to put two squads' velocities on the same slide, even when asked by someone senior, and who instead offers throughput in items or cycle-time percentiles. The obvious reading — that comparing teams is a reasonable management activity — destroys the only estimate the organisation had.

The epic is an accounting convenience, not a design object. An expert will kill an epic mid-flight with half its stories unbuilt and feel nothing, because the epic was never a commitment; the stories were. The tell is an epic closed with a one-line note saying the remaining slices are no longer worth building. The obvious reading treats the epic as a mini-project with an implied completion obligation, which is how organisations end up finishing features that nobody wanted by the time the fourth slice shipped.

Demonstrable and releasable are different properties, and vertical slicing guarantees only the first. Gadya could demonstrate the UPI reconciliation flow on a bench terminal in week two; it could not release it to forty-one thousand devices until June. An expert holds these apart in language, in the definition of done, and in what they promise a stakeholder. The tell is a demo that opens with an explicit statement of what is and is not releasable. The obvious reading collapses them and produces the worst kind of stakeholder surprise: a feature that was shown working in March and reaches customers in July.

The hardest and most valuable split removes a quality attribute rather than a feature. "Works for ten concurrent admissions clerks" and "works for four hundred" are two stories, and the first is genuinely shippable to a pilot. Most teams never think of this axis because non-functional requirements feel like constraints rather than content. The tell is a backlog containing a story whose only difference from an earlier one is a number in a performance criterion. The obvious reading treats scale as something you either have or do not have, which forces every performance question into the largest, least tractable slice.

Story splitting is a negotiation instrument pointed at your own stakeholders as much as at engineers. A split backlog lets a product manager say "these four slices by 1 April, these three after" to a customer or a CEO, which is a conversation the undifferentiated epic makes impossible. The tell is a product manager who brings the post-split table — not the roadmap — into a commercial conversation. The obvious reading, that slicing is an engineering hygiene practice, misses that its largest organisational payoff is the ability to make a partial promise credibly.

7. How this changes across product types and company stages

Some of the differences commonly asserted here are real and some are folklore, and it is worth separating them. In consumer products, slices are small, personas are plentiful, and the binding constraint is usually experiment throughput rather than specification: the story is a lightweight wrapper around a hypothesis, and a great deal of the apparatus can be dispensed with because a wrong slice is cheap. In B2B and enterprise, of which Granthik is a clean example, the same slice must satisfy fewer, more idiosyncratic customers, and acceptance criteria migrate from an internal artefact to a quasi-contractual one — a customer's technical contact may read them before a renewal. This is the single largest genuine difference: in consumer products acceptance criteria are written for testers, in enterprise they are written for testers and auditors and procurement, and the third audience changes the prose.

For platform work the story format degrades honestly, because the user of a platform slice is another engineering team and the "so that" clause becomes a statement about future optionality that cannot be verified now. Mature platform teams substitute a consumer-driven contract: the slice is defined by an API contract that a named client team has agreed to adopt within a stated window, and if no such client exists, the slice is not built. In marketplaces the two-sided problem described above dominates, and the practical adaptation is paired stories with a joint acceptance boundary.

In hardware and physical goods, the operative variable is the release clock rather than the product type, and Sneha's rule generalises: push judgement up the stack to whichever layer ships fastest, and keep the slow-clock slices few, large and conservative. For AI products, as the Gaatha Voice episode showed, the specification unit itself is contested; the working substitution is an evaluation set standing where the acceptance criterion stood.

Company stage matters in a way that is often overstated and occasionally understated. Overstated: the claim that early-stage companies should not write acceptance criteria. What early-stage companies should not do is write many of them; two falsifiable criteria cost ten minutes and prevent the most common argument. Understated: the change in who the backlog is for. At nine people, a backlog is a team's shared memory. At Granthik's three hundred and forty, it is also the instrument through which four squads, a QA function, a customer success team and eleven hospital chains hold a common model of what is coming — and at that point the cost of a badly-written story is paid by people who will never meet its author. That, rather than any change in the practice's mechanics, is what makes rigour worth paying for later and wasteful earlier.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

Granthik: a split that held under pressure

Arvind's twenty-two stories totalled 144 points against a five-sprint runway of 460 points of gross capacity. He committed only 288 points of it to the pre-auth epic, reserving the rest for the support load, an unrelated NABH documentation item, and a deliberate twenty-two percent buffer. In sprint two, the NHCX sandbox returned a payload field Granthik's integration layer had not anticipated, adding 13 points of unplanned work. Because it landed inside one slice of twenty-two rather than inside a 102-point monolith, the re-plan took one conversation: slices 17 through 19, covering two low-volume insurers, moved out of the April release and into July, and Arvind told the chain's CIO on 9 February — seven weeks before go-live — exactly which two insurers would come later. The chain accepted. The counterfactual is not hypothetical: on a previous project Granthik had discovered an equivalent surprise at integration testing in week nine and slipped a release by a quarter.

Gadya: a large slice chosen on purpose

Sneha's firmware slice was a single 34-point item that no textbook would approve of: it did four things at once and could not be demonstrated to a shopkeeper until the app layer existed. Her justification was the arithmetic of Table 3. Splitting it into three firmware candidates would have cost three verification cycles at roughly ₹9 lakh and five weeks each, delivering a feature that shipped in the same June window either way. The software layers above it were split into nineteen stories averaging three days of cycle time, and between February and June those nineteen went through four substantive redesigns based on observation at eleven pilot stores — redesigns that cost nothing precisely because the firmware below them had been made generic rather than opinionated.

Table 3. Gadya Retail Devices: the cost of slicing across versus below the firmware boundary, as presented by Sneha Kulkarni on 19 January 2026. Verification cost covers regression across eleven hardware revisions plus external re-verification where the weighing path is touched.

Gaatha Voice: where the practice failed, and what recovery looked like

Ritwik Mohanty's seven stories all shipped and containment fell seventeen points. The diagnosis, which took his team three weeks and a hundred and forty listened-to call recordings, was that each acceptance criterion had been verified against a handful of hand-written examples, and the hand-written examples had all been articulate, single-intent, and in one language. Real calls to an NBFC's borrowers were none of those things. Worse, the slices interacted: the consent-capture story and the eligibility-check story each independently added a confirmation turn, and nobody had owned the composed conversation because no story described it.

The recovery was not a return to bigger stories. It was a change in what a story was allowed to claim. Gaatha Voice built an evaluation set of six hundred and forty recorded and transcribed calls, stratified by language, intent and audio quality, and scored by a rubric two operations staff had agreed on. A story thereafter consisted of a change plus a predicted movement on a named subset of that eval set, and its acceptance criterion was a threshold on that movement — with a mandatory shadow-mode period on live traffic before any change reached callers. Containment recovered to fifty-four percent over the following quarter and reached sixty-one by the end of it. The instructive part is the cost of catching it late: four sprints of engineering, a quarter of degraded service to two lender clients, and one contract that went to renewal at reduced scope. Everything in the process had been done correctly according to the practice, which is exactly why nobody noticed for four sprints.

9. Failure modes, their early warning signs, and the cost of catching them late

Point inflation. The early warning is velocity rising while shipped user-visible behaviour is flat; the diagnostic question is "how many items did we finish, and has that number moved?"; the cost of catching it late is that every forecast built on velocity for the preceding two quarters was wrong in the same direction, usually optimistic, and the credibility loss lands on the product manager rather than the team.

Normalised carry-over. The warning is that more than a fifth of sprint items have been carried at least once; the diagnostic is "what is the age of the oldest in-progress item, in days?"; the cost of catching it late is that sprint boundaries have quietly become fictional, so the organisation has lost its only regular checkpoint without noticing.

Enabler colonisation. The warning is a rising share of sprint capacity going to items with no user in them; the diagnostic is "which user-visible slice does this enable, and in which sprint does that slice land?"; caught late, the team has spent a quarter building infrastructure for a feature that was cancelled in month two.

Criteria written after the code. The warning is acceptance criteria that describe implementation details no product person would have thought of; the diagnostic is "was this written before the branch was opened?"; the cost is that the criteria now prove only that the code does what it does.

Fake verticals. The warning is a backlog containing "part 1 of 3" chains; the diagnostic is "can I demo part 1 alone to someone outside engineering?"; late, this is horizontal layering with story labels, and it surfaces as three consecutive sprint reviews with nothing to show.

Epics that never close. The warning is an epic older than two quarters with items still being added to it; the diagnostic is "what would have to be true for us to close this epic unfinished?"; the cost of catching it late is a backlog that has become a graveyard nobody can prioritise against, because the epic's original rationale is no longer legible to anyone still on the team.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Estimate or right-size. The estimation camp argues that the act of estimating surfaces disagreement that would otherwise stay hidden, and that the number, imperfect as it is, lets a product manager make partial commitments to a business. Its evidence is Arvind's February conversation with the chain's CIO, which required a number. The right-sizing camp argues that cycle-time percentiles forecast at least as well at a fraction of the cost, and that estimation's supposed conversational benefit can be had by simply having the conversation. Its evidence is the repeated finding that item counts predict elapsed time about as well as point sums. What would have to be true for the right-sizing camp to be wrong: that the variance of item sizes within a team's backlog is large and irreducible, so counting genuinely loses information. In Granthik's regulated, heterogeneous backlog that may well be true; in Gadya's cloud squad it plainly was not. Neither camp has conceded, and both are behaving rationally given their own data.

Who holds the pen. One position holds that the product manager writes the story because only the product manager owns the user's interest and the trade-offs against other work. The other holds that a story written by someone who will not build it is a specification in disguise, and that the three-amigos practice — product, engineering and testing drafting together — produces better slices and eliminates the handover defect class entirely. What would have to be true for the collaborative position to be wrong: that the coordination cost of three people drafting exceeds the cost of the misunderstandings it prevents, which is plausible on a distributed team spanning eight time zones and implausible in one room.

Whether the story is the right unit above a certain scale. The story-mapping tradition holds that flat backlogs destroy the narrative that makes prioritisation possible, and that the remedy is a map, not a hierarchy. The scaled-framework tradition holds that above roughly a hundred engineers the binding constraint is funding and sequencing across teams, which requires explicit levels above the story and a common economic ordering rule. Each has evidence: mapping advocates point to backlogs of nine hundred items that no human can reason about; framework advocates point to organisations where three teams independently built the same capability. What would have to be true for the hierarchy position to be wrong: that the coordination it buys could be had by co-locating ownership instead — which is exactly what Arvind did at a scale of twenty-seven engineers, and exactly what does not obviously work at three hundred.

Whether AI-native products can be specified as stories at all. One camp holds that they can, that an evaluation threshold is simply a more sophisticated acceptance criterion, and that the discipline is otherwise unchanged. The other holds that behavioural specification is category-inappropriate for systems whose quality is distributional, and that the right unit is a capability plus an eval suite plus a rollout gate, with stories demoted to implementation tasks. Gaatha Voice's recovery is consistent with both readings, which is precisely why the disagreement persists. What would settle it is evidence about whether teams using eval-gated stories actually catch composition failures — the four-confirmations-in-two-minutes class — that pointwise criteria miss. As of now that evidence is anecdotal on both sides.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this practice writes stories that pass INVEST. Someone who has internalised it does four things differently. They ask about feedback latency before they ask about sprint capacity, because they know which of the two arguments for slicing is available to them. They know their own team's splitting inflation number and their own cycle-time percentiles, and they use them to decide when to stop splitting rather than appealing to a rule. They abandon the apparatus without anxiety — dropping the template on stories where the user is obvious, dropping points where right-sizing is cheaper, keeping a large slice when the integration cost per slice is high and saying why — while never abandoning the four slice properties, because those are the part that carries the argument. And they treat the backlog as an instrument of external negotiation rather than internal hygiene: the test is whether they can walk into a customer conversation and make a credible partial promise, which is a thing a fourteen-page specification has never once enabled anyone to do.

12. What Arvind and Sneha decided

Arvind adopted Cut B on 16 January: twenty-two stories sliced by insurer and procedure category, each spanning payload, interface and audit trail, with Integrations named as the integrating owner and two Platform engineers loaned for the duration. He wrote the forty-one percent inflation figure into the plan document so that nobody would later read the velocity rise as a productivity gain, and he spent real political capital negotiating the two-hospital fortnightly pilot, which was the only part of the plan that bought him any learning at all. He shipped nineteen of twenty-two slices by 1 April and told the CIO about the other three seven weeks in advance. His reasoning, written into Granthik's wiki, was not that slicing made the work smaller — it made it larger by forty-one percent — but that it converted an unknowable ninety-four-day risk into a sequence of two-week risks he could report on honestly.

Sneha did the opposite below the firmware line and the same thing above it. One conservative, generic 34-point firmware slice; nineteen thin, revisable slices in the app and cloud layers; a deliberate forty percent engineering premium paid to keep product judgement off the slow clock. She shipped in the June window, after four redesigns that cost nothing because they never touched firmware. Asked at an internal review why she had refused to split the firmware work, she gave an answer worth remembering: slicing is not a virtue, it is a purchase — you are buying variance reduction and optionality, and you should know the price before you buy.

Discussion questions

1. Arvind accepted a forty-one percent increase in total estimated effort to reduce forecast variance from roughly twenty-six percent to under ten. Under what conditions is that trade wrong — and would you have made it if the go-live date had been six months out rather than eleven weeks?

2. Sneha pushed product judgement up to the fastest-shipping layer at a forty percent engineering premium. Is that a slicing decision, an architecture decision, or the same decision wearing two labels — and who in your organisation is accountable for it?

3. Gaatha Voice's seven stories were, by every published standard, correctly written. If the practice cannot detect a failure of composition, is the right conclusion that the practice needs a new artefact, or that the unit of specification for AI-native products is simply not the story?

13. Going deeper

PRD structure
The artefact stories are cut from; understanding which parts of a PRD survive the cut and which are context-only tells you how much specification work is genuinely reusable.
Backlog management and refinement
Slicing is a single act; refinement is the ongoing discipline that keeps a twenty-two-item backlog alive, reordered and re-estimated as reality disagrees with January. This is the direct sequel.
PM artefacts: one-pager, PRD, spec, strategy doc
Placing the story in the artefact hierarchy stops the common error of asking a story to carry an argument that belongs in a strategy document.
Writing a one-pager
The upstream decision — whether to build at all — that story slicing is silent about and can dangerously appear to have answered.
Customer narratives (Day 0 / Day N)
The narrative form that story maps preserve and flat backlogs destroy; useful precisely where the epic hierarchy loses the sequence a user actually experiences.
Acceptance criteria and error cases
The falsifiability contract at the heart of section 3, taken seriously: boundary values, error paths, and the criteria that regulated products cannot negotiate.
Telemetry requirements
Without instrumentation written into the slice, the learning leg of the slicing argument is unavailable even where feedback latency is short.
Non-functional requirements
The quality-attribute split is the hardest and most valuable one; this topic supplies the vocabulary for slicing scale, latency and availability as content rather than constraint.

Granthik Health Systems, Gadya Retail Devices and Gaatha Voice are illustrative composites constructed for teaching purposes; the regulatory and market institutions referred to are real and appear only as context.

User Stories and Epics: Cutting a Spec Into Pieces a Team Can Actually Finish

How does a product manager turn a fourteen-page requirements document into work that a six-person engineering team can pull off a backlog, build in a fortnight, and ship without anyone discovering — three days before launch — that nobody agreed on what "done" meant?

1. A Diwali deadline and a document nobody can build from

On the morning of 6 October 2025, Fareed Khan, VP of Product at the Bengaluru test-prep company Falak Learning, printed out the Personalised Revision Planner PRD and read it twice before the 10 a.m. sprint planning call. It was a good document by most measures: fourteen pages, a clear problem statement, three user personas, a table of edge cases, and a diagram of how the recommendation engine should weight a student's recent quiz scores against a syllabus calendar. Falak's flagship product, an app used by roughly 340,000 students preparing for engineering and medical entrance exams, had lost market share over the summer to a faster-moving Pune rival, and the leadership team had set an unforgiving date: the revision planner had to be live before the Diwali surge in November, when new sign-ups traditionally tripled.

The problem was not the PRD's quality. The problem was that it described an outcome — "students receive a daily revision plan personalised to their weak topics" — and said almost nothing about how six engineers, with a combined capacity of roughly 40 story points per three-week sprint, were supposed to turn that outcome into a sequence of things they could build, test, and ship one at a time. When Fareed had tried this once before, on a smaller feature, the team had spent the first two weeks of a six-week build gold-plating the recommendation algorithm before anyone had touched the screen a student would actually see, and the feature slipped by five weeks. Riya Sen, Falak's engineering lead, put it bluntly on a call the week before: "Give me a PRD and I'll give you a debate. Give me stories and I'll give you a sprint." Fareed's task that morning was to decide, with the whole roadmap now compressed into seven working weeks, exactly how to slice the planner into pieces small enough to pull, order, and finish — without losing the coherence of what the planner was supposed to do.

2. The idea, stated precisely

A user story is a short, deliberately incomplete description of one thing a specific kind of user can now do, written in a stock form — as a <role>, I want <goal>, so that <benefit> — that is small enough for a development team to design, build, test, and demonstrate within a single sprint, and that is meant to be filled out through conversation between the person who wrote it and the people who will build it, rather than through the story text alone. An epic is simply a story that is still too large to do that: a container for an outcome the team agrees matters, held at a coarser grain until someone splits it into stories a sprint can absorb.

The format was popularised inside the Extreme Programming community that Kent Beck and Ward Cunningham were building at Chrysler's C3 payroll project in the late 1990s, as a reaction against requirements documents that were exhaustive, expensive to maintain, and usually stale by the time engineers read them. Beck's insight, later systematised by Mike Cohn in his 2004 book User Stories Applied, was that a written requirement is not a contract to be executed literally; it is what Ron Jeffries later called "a promise of a conversation" — a reminder to talk, at build time, to the person who actually needs the thing, rather than a substitute for that talk. Cohn also gave the discipline its most durable diagnostic, the INVEST checklist: a good story should be Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, and Testable. Fareed's version of the idea, the sentence he could say in a leadership review without sounding like he was reciting a framework, was this: a story is the smallest slice of the planner that a student could actually use and that Riya's team could actually finish in one sprint; an epic is what they call that same slice before they have cut it down to that size.

"INVEST is not a grammar rule for writing sentences that start with 'As a user.' It is a test for whether the team can actually finish the thing inside one sprint without secretly depending on four other things finishing first." — working note from Falak's engineering wiki, attributed to Riya Sen

3. The mechanics, walked through

Splitting a PRD into stories is a sequence of decisions, and most teams skip several of them without noticing, which is exactly where the practice breaks down. Fareed's team, coached by Riya, walked the Personalised Revision Planner through six steps.

Step one: name the epics. They read the PRD and pulled out the handful of outcomes it actually promised, each one large enough to need its own sequence of stories but small enough to be a coherent thread: "student sees a daily revision plan," "student's plan updates after a new quiz," "student can mark a topic mastered and see the plan adapt," and "coach dashboard shows a cohort's revision coverage." Four epics, not fourteen pages of prose.

Step two: write the first story in each epic in the role-goal-benefit form. This step is where teams most often go through the motions without doing the thinking, because the format is easy to fill in badly. "As a user, I want a revision plan, so that I can study" tells the engineer nothing they didn't already know. Riya's team insisted on a rule Fareed adopted: the role had to be a real persona from the PRD (a Class 12 NEET aspirant six weeks from her exam, not "a user"), and the benefit had to name the thing that would actually change for her, not restate the goal in different words.

Step three: attach acceptance criteria. Each story got three to six concrete, testable conditions, usually in Given/When/Then form, that said exactly what "done" meant — because the step teams leave implicit is deciding, before a line of code is written, what a QA engineer will actually check. A story without acceptance criteria is a title, not a commitment.

Step four: apply INVEST as a filter, not a checklist to tick. A story that touched both the recommendation algorithm and the UI that displayed it failed "independent" — it could not be estimated or tested on its own, so it had to be split again along that seam.

Step five: split the epic using a splitting pattern, not by instinct. The patterns practitioners actually reach for are workflow steps (split along the sequence a user follows), business rules (split one version of a rule from another — "recommend the top-1 weak topic" before "recommend a ranked list weighted by exam proximity"), data boundaries (one subject before all five), CRUD operations (view a plan before edit a plan), and happy path before edge cases (a student with quiz history before a brand-new student with none). Falak's team used workflow steps first, then business-rule variants within each step.

Step six: estimate and order. Each finished story was sized in story points — a relative unit of effort and uncertainty, not hours — using a Fibonacci-like scale (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13) and a round of "planning poker" where engineers reveal estimates simultaneously to avoid anchoring on the first number spoken. The product manager then orders the backlog by value against cost, not by the sequence the PRD happened to describe things in.

4. The arithmetic Fareed actually had to do

The "student sees a daily revision plan" epic, once split by workflow step and business-rule variant, produced nine candidate stories. Riya's team estimated each one in story points during a ninety-minute poker session on 8 October. The table below is close to what came out of that session, reordered by the priority Fareed assigned once he had the estimates in front of him.

Table 1. Stories split from the "daily revision plan" epic, Falak Learning, sprint beginning 6 October 2025. Team capacity: 40 story points per three-week sprint.

Twenty-four points of "Must" work against 40 points of sprint-one capacity looked comfortable at first glance — until Fareed remembered that sprint one also had to carry roughly 8 points of unrelated bug-fix and on-call work that Riya's team always reserved, which the PRD had never mentioned because a PRD does not think in sprints. Twenty-four plus eight is 32, which still fits inside 40, so sprint one shipped stories 1 through 4 plus the reserved work, landing at 32 of 40 points — a deliberate 20 percent buffer, because Riya had been burned before by estimates that assumed a sprint with no interruptions.

Now change one input. Two weeks into planning, Falak's data science lead told Fareed that the "re-rank after each new quiz attempt" story (story 4, 8 points) actually depended on a model-serving pipeline that did not exist yet — a dependency nobody had surfaced in the original estimate, because the team had estimated the UI behaviour without checking whether the data behind it was ready. Once that dependency surfaced, story 4 grew from 8 points to an epic of its own: a 3-point "serve static top-3 ranking from yesterday's batch job" story that could ship in sprint one, and a deferred 8-point "live re-ranking" story that moved to sprint two. Sprint one's committed total fell from 32 to 27 points against the same 40-point capacity — and Fareed used the freed capacity to pull story 5, the exam-date weighting, forward from sprint two. The arithmetic is not decoration here: it is the only way Fareed could show his CEO, in the same 10 a.m. call where the fourteen-page PRD had produced nothing but debate, a specific, defensible answer to "what ships in three weeks."

5. Eight things a learner has to notice

A story is not a requirement in disguise.

A requirement asserts what the system must do; a story is a placeholder for a conversation about what a specific person needs, deliberately left underspecified until the team that will build it has had that conversation. Teams that write stories the way they used to write requirements — dense, exhaustive, final — have kept the label and lost the point.

Stories are not tasks, and epics are not projects.

A task is technical and internal ("add an index to the quiz_attempts table"); a story is user-facing and testable by someone outside engineering. An epic is a grouping of related value, sized in weeks, not a project with a Gantt chart — it has no separate budget, timeline, or owner beyond the stories inside it.

Story points measure effort and uncertainty together, not hours.

Two stories can both take a developer roughly six hours and still deserve different point values if one of them touches code nobody on the team has worked in for a year. Teams that convert points to hours ("1 point = 4 hours") quietly destroy the uncertainty signal the points existed to capture, and then wonder why estimates keep being wrong in the same direction.

INVEST is a diagnostic, not a law of nature.

A story can fail "independent" for a defensible reason — sometimes two stories genuinely must ship together — and the right response is a documented decision to combine them, not a forced, artificial split that produces two stories neither of which is independently valuable.

Splitting is not the same operation as prioritising.

Splitting decides how big a slice is; prioritising decides which slice goes first. Teams that conflate them tend to split epics in whatever order is easiest to write, then discover the resulting sequence does not match what the business actually needed first.

A story tells you what to build next, not whether to build it at all.

INVEST and story-splitting have nothing to say about whether the revision planner was the right feature for Falak to build this quarter — that is a discovery and prioritisation question, answered before a story is ever written, not by the story format itself.

"Vertical slice" is the discipline that makes the whole method work.

A slice that cuts through every layer of the system — UI, logic, data — for one thin piece of behaviour is a real story; a slice that delivers "the database schema" in one sprint and "the API" in the next is a horizontal layer, demoable to no one, and the single most common way teams sabotage story splitting without realising it.

Acceptance criteria and definition of done are not the same list.

Acceptance criteria are specific to one story ("the flagged topic is the one with the lowest of the student's last three quiz scores"); definition of done is a standing, team-wide bar every story must clear regardless of content (code reviewed, tests passing, accessibility checked). Teams that fold one into the other end up with acceptance criteria too generic to test against and a definition of done that changes every sprint.

6. How the same idea looks different by product type and company stage

Falak Learning is a consumer product, and its stories read like the ones above: single-user, single-session, framed around one student's next action. A B2B counterpart looks different in a way that matters. At Firoza Systems, a Chandigarh-based freight-management SaaS company selling to logistics operators, a comparable story reads "as a fleet dispatcher managing forty trucks, I want the revision — no, in Firoza's case, the route-reassignment — plan to respect a driver's daily hours-of-service limit, so that I do not get fined by a state transport authority." The persona is a professional role inside a customer organisation rather than an end consumer, the benefit clause usually cites a compliance or cost consequence rather than a personal one, and acceptance criteria routinely need to reference a specific customer's configuration, because B2B products serve fewer, more different customers than consumer products serve many similar ones. A marketplace product splits differently again: because a marketplace has at least two sides, Falak's hypothetical marketplace cousin — a platform connecting NEET coaches to students for one-on-one doubt-clearing sessions — needs separate epics for the coach-facing and student-facing halves of what looks like one feature, and a story is rarely complete until both sides have been written, because a supply-side story that ships without its matching demand-side story changes nothing a user can actually experience.

Company stage matters just as much as product type. At an early-stage company — Falak two years earlier, when it was nine people building the first version of its quiz engine — epics rarely survived more than a sprint or two before the whole plan changed, because the team was still discovering which persona and which problem mattered, and writing exhaustive acceptance criteria for a story that might not exist next week was wasted effort; a looser, single-sentence story with a conversation at pickup time was the right amount of process. At Falak's current size — sixty people, a dedicated QA function, and paying institutional customers who signed SLAs — the same looseness would be negligent: acceptance criteria had become the artefact QA tested against, product management against, and, increasingly, the artefact a coaching-institute customer's technical contact asked to see before a contract renewal. The story format does not change; how much weight the organisation is willing to put on it does.

7. Where teams go wrong, and how you would catch it from outside

The first common mistake is the story that is really a requirements paragraph wearing a costume: "As a user, I want the system to support personalised recommendations, so that engagement improves." The symptom, visible from outside the team, is that the story survives three sprints without anyone finishing it, because it was never small enough to finish. The underlying misunderstanding is treating the role-goal-benefit sentence as a formatting exercise rather than as a forcing function for scope. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask, in fifteen seconds, "can you show me this working, end to end, for one real user, by Friday?" — if the answer is no, it is an epic wearing a story's clothes.

The second is horizontal splitting, described above: schema this sprint, API next sprint, UI the sprint after. The symptom is a string of sprint demos with nothing to show a stakeholder. The misunderstanding is thinking of a story as a chunk of the codebase rather than a chunk of user-visible behaviour. The diagnostic is to check whether any story in the current sprint can be demoed to someone outside engineering; if none can, the split happened along the wrong axis.

The third is estimating a story before its dependencies are known, the way Falak's re-ranking story was estimated at 8 points before anyone checked whether the model-serving pipeline existed. The symptom is a story that blows through its estimate mid-sprint for reasons that, in hindsight, were knowable beforehand. The misunderstanding is treating estimation as a property of the story text alone rather than of the story plus its technical context. The diagnostic is a standing habit Riya's team adopted after the incident: no story enters a sprint without one named technical owner confirming, out loud, that its dependencies are either already built or explicitly scoped as part of the story.

The fourth is writing acceptance criteria so vague they cannot fail — "the plan should be personalised and useful" — which produces the symptom of QA and engineering disagreeing about whether a story is done, discovered only at sprint review. The underlying error is writing criteria to satisfy the story-writing ritual rather than to give a tester something falsifiable. The cheap diagnostic: hand the acceptance criteria to someone who was not in the room when they were written and ask them to test the story; if they cannot, without asking a clarifying question, tell whether a given behaviour passes or fails, the criteria are not acceptance criteria yet.

8. What it looks like done well

By the second week of October, Falak's backlog for the Personalised Revision Planner had a shape Fareed was willing to defend in front of the board: four epics, each broken into stories no larger than 8 points, each story carrying two to five acceptance criteria phrased so a QA engineer with no context could test them, and a sprint-one commitment of 27 points against 40 of capacity that left visible room for the unknowns a fourteen-page PRD could never have surfaced. Riya's team could look at any single story and answer, without consulting Fareed, whether it was ready to pull. When the model-serving dependency surfaced mid-planning, the team absorbed it in a single conversation and a same-day re-estimate rather than a renegotiation of the whole roadmap, because the stories were small enough that one of them changing did not destabilise the rest. That is the practical payoff of the discipline: not a prettier document, but a backlog that bends instead of breaking when reality disagrees with the plan.

9. What Fareed decided

Fareed shipped sprint one on schedule, with stories 1 through 3 and the reduced-scope version of story 4, on 24 October 2025 — twelve days before the Diwali traffic surge Falak's leadership had been anticipating since August. He kept the exam-date weighting story and the coach-override story in the visible backlog rather than deferring them to a vague "phase two," because a backlog a stakeholder can see and reorder is more honest than a phase label that quietly becomes a promise. The reasoning he wrote into Falak's product wiki afterward was not a claim that story-splitting had made the planner easier to build — it had not; the model-serving dependency was real work regardless of how it was sliced. The claim he made was narrower and, he thought, more defensible: slicing the epic into independently demoable stories had made the team's actual progress visible three weeks earlier than a PRD ever could have, and had turned one unpleasant surprise into a same-day adjustment instead of a five-week slip. The next thing on Fareed's list to learn, and the topic this one unlocks, is backlog management and refinement — the ongoing discipline of keeping a backlog like Table 1 alive, reordered, and re-estimated as a living artefact, rather than a plan written once in October and never revisited.

Two questions worth sitting with:

1. When you last wrote a "story" that took your team three sprints to finish, was the format the problem, or had you quietly slipped back into writing a requirement and calling it a story?

2. If a dependency like Falak's model-serving pipeline surfaced inside your current sprint's largest story, would your team notice it in a single conversation — or only at the sprint review, when it is too late to do anything but slip the date?

Falak Learning and Firoza Systems are used here as illustrative composites for teaching purposes.

Section 1Sunday night

At 10.20 p.m. on Sunday, 15 November 2026, Neelima Yellamraju had four windows open on a kitchen table in Bengaluru and no way to reconcile them: a Pune capacity sheet putting thirty-five engineer-weeks between Monday and code-complete; a Singapore extract arguing that twenty-three of the ninety-four requirements have an India analogue barely anyone uses; an email from New Jersey titled Annexure C is not negotiable; and a slide rewritten nine times, Re-baselined plan, SOW-2.

At 9 a.m. IST on Monday, Gananam Systems owed Gharoob Retail Group's programme office in Dubai a re-baselined plan for the programme signed in August. At 6.30 p.m. IST she was to speak for eleven minutes to a board sub-committee told in September that the programme was on track, and nothing since.

The contract described ninety-four numbered requirements. Her engineers described five epics. Her designer in Berlin described two products. Yellamraju had spent eleven years learning to turn a specification into pieces a team could pull and finish; nobody had told her what to do when the pieces arrived numbered, priced and signed.

Section 2The company, and the clause that still governs it

Gananam Systems Private Limited was founded in Bengaluru in 2016 out of a decade of distribution ERP for Indian FMCG wholesalers. By the year ended 31 March 2026 it had ₹186 crore of annual recurring revenue, 640 employees in Bengaluru and Pune, and 1,180 distributor firms with 40,870 named users.

The decision that governs this case was taken on Friday, 17 March 2023. Gharoob Retail Group — 212 stores and three distribution centres in the UAE and Oman, Indian-founded, Dubai-headquartered — would sign Gananam's first Gulf contract only on its own paper, and that paper carried Annexure C: every requirement a numbered line item, acceptance per item, each payment milestone tied to a range of numbers. Nishchal Yeddanapudi, then selling the Gulf from New Jersey, argued that a Dubai reference account was worth it.

Annexure C, or a clause copied from it, now sits in nine of Gananam's fourteen enterprise contracts, carrying ₹74 crore of the ₹186 crore of ARR, or 39.8 per cent. By 2024 Gananam's engineers were pulling thin vertical slices through a shared ledger. Annexure C bills in horizontal ranges.

Section 3The industry

Zoho, Freshworks and Postman established that a product built in Chennai or Bengaluru can be sold in Dubai. Gananam sits downstream of Indian payments plumbing — UPI and NPCI made collection against an invoice a one-tap event, GST e-invoicing made the invoice machine-readable — and upstream of a trade squeezed by Reliance Retail and Metro, by Udaan and Jumbotail, and by Zepto and Swiggy Instamart, which have taught retailers to expect credit terms their distributors never gave.

Credit is where regulation bites, in two places. In India, embedded lending must flow through an entity the Reserve Bank of India regulates, so Gananam's credit module runs against an RBI-registered NBFC partner, with consent flows built to that shape and personal data handled under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. In the UAE the lender must be licensed by the Central Bank of the UAE, VAT applies at 5 per cent on the invoice line, and the terms that matter commercially stretch across Ramadan. Gharoob pays ₹3.78 crore a year for the order-capture product live since 5 February 2024 — 2.0 per cent of ARR, 5.1 per cent of Annexure C ARR — and the receivables programme adds a ₹4.20 crore fee plus, on go-live, a ₹2.16 crore subscription uplift, taking the account to ₹5.94 crore. Behind it sits ₹31 crore of qualified Gulf pipeline across six prospects whose RFPs name Gharoob as reference site.

Section 4What happened, what was believed, and what has since turned out wrong

Statement of Work 2, Receivables, Collections and Credit, was signed on Friday, 28 August 2026. It carried the ninety-four requirement IDs, C-001 to C-094, and priced implementation at ₹4.20 crore against a pre-sales sizing of 44 engineer-weeks. Design sign-off was invoiced on 30 September 2026 and the 15 per cent advance of ₹63.00 lakh received. Build was to start 1 October.

It did not. Order volumes on the India platform roughly triple around Deepavali, which fell on Sunday, 8 November 2026, and Gananam freezes its India releases from mid-October to the first week of January, holding the platform squads on support; a DPDP consent-artefact remediation raised in September took the same consent service the Gharoob requirements need. Gharoob build now starts 16 November (Exhibit 1).

Three beliefs held in August have not survived. First, that the 44 engineer-weeks estimated the ninety-four requirements: Nandhan Yenugula's squad re-estimated them bottom-up between 2 and 11 November and returned 71, so the fee was priced against 61.97 per cent of the bottom-up figure, 44 of 71 (Exhibit 3). Third, that the India product already held most of what Gharoob wanted: Navamani Yerragudi's extract of 10 November (Exhibit 4) was circulated as evidence that it did, and Narmada Yethirajulu's reading of it is that it cannot carry the weight.
