Ethiyan and the Sixty-Two-Page Promise

A case on user stories and epics

1. Opening

On Monday 19 October 2026, Mirnalini Vedantam, Head of Product at Ethiyan Systems, sat in the Indiranagar office in Bengaluru with a printed 62-page document open to its last page. The product requirements document for "Order-linked credit" had been approved by the chief executive the previous Friday. It described a way for a kirana retailer to place an order with a distributor and pay fifteen days later, with a partner lender carrying the money in between.

Ethiyan's enterprise sales head, Murugesan Veluswamy, had already told three pilot distributors that the feature would reach them "for Diwali". Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November, and engineering froze releases from Friday 6 November until Monday 16 November. Sprint planning was on Friday 23 October. By then Mirnalini had to decide how the PRD would be cut into work the team could pull, and what Murugesan could truthfully promise.

2. Company background

Ethiyan was founded in Pune in 2019. Its product, Ethiyan Orders, is an app through which FMCG distributors take orders from kirana retailers, replacing the WhatsApp messages and phone calls that still carry most of that trade. By October 2026 it served 140 distributors in 22 cities and about 41,000 active retailers, at an average subscription of ₹60,000 a month per distributor, or annual recurring revenue of about ₹10 crore.

The competition was uneven. Udaan and Jumbotail ran their own wholesale marketplaces, and Khatabook and OkCredit kept retailers' ledgers. Ethiyan's pitch was to sit inside the distributor's business, not replace it. Credit was the gap. Retailers routinely asked distributors for fifteen or thirty days, distributors carried the risk on paper, and several larger distributors had begun asking whether Ethiyan could take over the arrangement under a regulated lender, within the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending rules. A partner non-banking finance company had agreed in principle. Its contract and API specification were not yet signed.

3. The situation

Mirnalini thought the PRD good. It covered six requirement areas, each written as prose with acceptance criteria at the back. Mugunthan Vinjamuri, her engineering manager, had spent a week estimating them; Exhibit 1 shows 112 engineer-days in total.

Capacity was the difficulty. Mugunthan's team had nine engineers across Pune and Bengaluru, but three were pinned to Diwali-season reliability and on-call. That left six to build. Work could begin on Monday 26 October and had to end by Thursday 5 November, which gave nine working days, or 54 engineer-days. From past sprints, he reckoned about 75 per cent of time went to story work rather than meetings, reviews and support, so 40.5 engineer-days was the usable figure.

The perspectives differed by location. In Bengaluru, the engineers asked to be given something they could finish. In Singapore, Manikya Vangala heard the retailers' side from support tickets. In New Jersey, Murugesan had given the pilot distributors a date. Time zones shaped the week: Friday's planning call would be at 7:30 pm in Bengaluru, 10:00 am in New Jersey, which was 9.5 hours behind India until clocks changed on 1 November, and 10:00 pm in Singapore.

4. The people

Mirnalini Vedantam, Head of Product, Bengaluru, owns the PRD's outcome and the decision. She wants a plan she can defend to the chief executive whether or not the date holds.

Mugunthan Vinjamuri, engineering manager, Pune, leads the nine engineers. He wants stories his team can pull, finish and demonstrate.

Murugesan Veluswamy, sales head, working from New Jersey, closed the three pilots. He believes "about half" of retailers want credit and that a demo at Diwali would let Ethiyan bring forward two other distributor renewals. He wants the full PRD by the freeze.

Manikya Vangala, customer-success lead, Singapore, runs support for all Ethiyan accounts. She is neutral on the date but sure that a retailer who gets credit and cannot see when to repay will phone her team within a day.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 sets Mugunthan's estimate against the PRD's six areas. The partner integration is the heaviest item, and its contract is unsigned.

6. The options

Option 1: slice by layer. Break the PRD into three epics along the technical stack: a back-end epic (partner integration, repayment collection, ledger and invoice: 30 + 22 + 14 = 66 engineer-days), an app epic (credit limit and order: 12 + 26 = 38) and an admin console epic (8). Each team member owns a layer, and the stories are written from the developer's point of view. It matches how the code is organised. It costs time to first use: at 4.5 usable engineer-days a day, the back-end epic alone needs about 14.7 working days, so no retailer can touch anything before the freeze.

Option 2: slice vertically. Cut thin end-to-end slices of the retailer's journey, each written as a story a person could demo, and carve eleven stories of two to four days from the 112-day estimate. Slice A, the retailer sees a pre-approved limit from a static file supplied by the lender, takes 8 days. Slice B, the retailer places a "pay later" order within the limit and the distributor sees its due date, takes 14. Slice C, the retailer repays through a Razorpay payment link settled by UPI, takes 16. Together they come to 38 engineer-days against 40.5. The remaining 74 days, including the live lender integration, stay in the backlog unpromised, and the first release covers Pune only, behind a switch. The cost is a manual lender file and a thinner product than the PRD describes.

Option 3: investigate first. Spend the nine days on a spike: sign the lender contract, test its sandbox and write down what the API really returns, then slice the PRD after the freeze. It moves the pilot to January and means telling three distributors that the Diwali date has gone, which Murugesan thinks puts the two renewals at risk.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1 and the capacity figure, how much of the PRD can the team finish before the freeze, and what may Murugesan promise on that basis?
  2. Which of the INVEST letters (independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small, testable), if any, does a story reading "Build the partner lender integration and KYC", the requirement area as printed in Exhibit 1, satisfy?
  3. Taking Exhibit 2 as evidence, what does a retailer in Pune need to be able to do in the first release to learn whether the idea works, and what can wait?
  4. Which option would you take to the planning call on Friday 23 October, what would you tell the Pune distributor, and what new fact would make you change course?

8. A note for the learner

An epic is a body of work too large to finish in one sprint, and a story is a slice small enough to pull, finish and show. The INVEST test checks a slice before it enters the backlog. A slice should be independent of its neighbours, negotiable in detail, valuable to a user, estimable, small, and testable. The case turns on the difference between slicing a spec by layer, which groups work by who builds it, and slicing by journey, which groups work by what a user can do afterwards.

One defensible path is Option 2. Exhibit 1 shows 112 days against 40.5 usable, so the Diwali promise cannot be the PRD. It can be a working loop of limit, order and repayment, which is what Slices A to C amount to. Each of the eleven stories is a size the team can finish in a few days and show to Manikya's team, and the 2.5 unallocated days are a sensible margin on estimates made in a week.
